observation: The current runtime candidate exposes ClayRuntime.mint_capability(kind) as a directly callable method. Its handle validation is strongly fail-closed after minting, but post-mint unforgeability alone does not prove that untrusted/model/guest code cannot reach the mint root.
non_claim: This run does NOT claim an exploitable production vulnerability. Exposure of the ClayRuntime object/mint method to model or guest code was not established from current evidence.

hypothesis.claim: Capability minting must be controlled by a trust root that is not reachable through the model-generated ClayCode/guest adapter surface. Model code may request/propose a capability, but only an external policy/authority path may cause issuance.
hypothesis.prediction: A guest-facing API inventory contains invoke/use/attenuate operations as allowed but no unrestricted mint/grant root. Attempts by model/guest code to call or synthesize the mint path fail before a live capability is created.
hypothesis.falsifier: The actual runtime/lowering architecture already proves mint_capability is unreachable from all untrusted/model-generated paths, or an alternative issuer design provides equivalent root isolation and this is covered by executable negative tests.

counterhypothesis: Keeping mint_capability on ClayRuntime is safe if ClayRuntime is a trusted host object never exposed to guest/model code; naming/public visibility in Python is not itself a security boundary failure.
discriminating_tests: Inventory the exact model-facing and compiled-Clay runtime ABI. Prove no route exposes ClayRuntime or a mint/grant callable.
Add a negative test whose guest/model surface attempts capability minting by name/reflection/adapter lookup and receives no live handle.
Pass pre-authorized capabilities into execution from a separate trusted bootstrap/issuer and show normal effects still work.
Revoke/rotate the issuer epoch and prove stale handles fail without making the issuer object reachable.
If cross-process FFI exists, prove the receiver can only use transferred/attenuated broker handles, not mint new authority.

implementation_candidates.shape: Separate CapabilityIssuer/Broker from ClayRuntime. Trusted bootstrap owns issuer; guest-facing runtime receives only a validation/use facade and selected handles.
advantages: maps naturally to broker/table capability models
implementation_candidates.risk: more plumbing; avoid unnecessary process split if one-module runtime can keep issuer in the same process but inaccessible to guest semantics

implementation_candidates.shape: Require an unexported root authority object/token to mint; runtime API without that object cannot issue capabilities.
implementation_candidates.risk: Python-level privacy is not a security boundary if arbitrary Python objects/reflection are exposed; must rely on the actual guest/lowering isolation model

implementation_candidates.shape: Bootstrap creates/installs attenuated capability handles in an instance-local table. Guest receives only opaque indices/handles and may never access the issuer root.
implementation_candidates.risk: table lifetime/ownership/revocation semantics must be specified and fuzzed

external_precedent: WASI distinguishes host/link-time provision of capabilities from runtime unforgeable handles. This supports testing issuer separation but does not dictate ClayCode's exact implementation.
promotion_guard: Do not promote until the actual production guest/model surface is inventoried and executable negative mint-root tests pass.
